7.16.m: Sanatkumāra said: / When that army was being slain by the gods together with the lords of the Pramathas, / the twenty-four terrible and proud dānavas became enraged: / Prahrāda, Anuhrāda, Saṃhrāda, Śini, Bāṣkala, / Jambha, Virocana, Vṛtra, Bali, Bāṇa, Aviniñjaya, / likewise Tuhuṇḍa, Huṇḍa, Śambhu, Kārtasvana, Kubha, / Śambara, Vipracitti, Ilvaka, Pilvaka, / Maya, Tāra, Tārakākṣa, Vidyunmālī, and Pramohana. / These twenty-four dānavas, overcome with fury, / rushed toward the armed divine Nandī who stood ready. / They, resembling mountains of collyrium, struck Nandī, who resembled a mountain of gold, / with tridents, spears, pikes, and paṭṭiśas. / Thus struck and hemmed in by those enemies with weapons, / Nandī was not shaken then, nor did he experience pain or suffering. / Then the lord, drawing his large drawn bow, / quickly pierced all the foremost dānavas with three arrows each. / Flowing with blood from the wounds made by arrows, those dānavas / shone like lordly mountains pouring forth streams of melted gold. / Then Nandī, puffed up with rage, with terrible arrows dispatched Kārttasvana, / who had been revived by Śukra, to the abode of Yama. / Reaching the end of his life, that great mountain of a dānava / fell down swiftly like a mountain struck by a thunderbolt, its stones shattered. / As he fell to the earth, killed, struck by Nandī's arrows, / Bali, having torn up a mountain peak, hurled it aiming at Nandī.

7.16.m: That slope of the mountain, complete with minerals, deer, predatory beasts, bears, and trees, / and filled with whirled-about stones and trees, rushed toward the lord of the gaṇas. / The beasts of prey and others swiftly departed from that peak thrown by Bali, / like relatives departing from a man overcome by misfortune. / That falling mountain peak the valiant Nandī / split with an arrow and roared, like a great wind scattering clouds. / Having split that mountain peak, the dweller on the mountain peak, / powerful, pierced Bali with an arrow as if [piercing] an arising obstacle. / Struck by the lord of the gaṇas, that son of Prahlāda, helpless, / fell suddenly to the earth like a tree struck down by the wind. / Then, when Bali fell, struck by Nandī's excellent arrow, / the dānavas, tormented by arrows, abandoned the battle from afar. / Then Andhaka, whose form resembled a rain-cloud, descended from the sky to the earth / toward those [demons] who resembled dispersed clouds, and spoke these words to the dānavas: / 'O sons of Diti, listen today to my words, / and carry out what is beneficial as spoken by me, if you approve. / You were born in noble families, heroic, and determined in the use of all weapons; / why do you flee, agitated by sharp iron arrows? / Where is that boasting of yours and what was spoken in the assembly? / Where is that excessive enmity of yours against the deities now? / Defeated by Nandī alone by hundreds and thousands, / how does shame not arise in you who boast in your domestic courtyards? / Turn back, you who know not unrighteousness! Fight! What is the use of fleeing? / There is no place where death does not come to us.'

7.16.m:
"Stand aside as arbiters, free from enmity and jealousy,
and witness now this single combat with Nandī!"
Hearing these words of Andhaka, all those Dānavas in battle
turned back once more to fight, seizing their excellent weapons.
Then mounting another chariot, a full nalva in size and adorned with banners,
Andhaka advanced against Nandī along with the foremost Dānavas.
Fierce, tipped with sharp gold, broad and fair to behold,
great arrows shot from Andhaka’s bow flew forth,
like locusts over fields, like bees upon trees,
like clouds around mountain lords, or like monsters in the ocean.
By the great arrows released, equal in splendor to serpents and the sun,
the gods were made by Andhaka like broken […]
Just as winds cannot be hindered, as death and old age cannot be stayed,
and as the blessings of brahmins, rightly uttered, are ever irresistible,
so those sharp, terrible great arrows of Andhaka,
like raised staffs of Brahmā, were unstoppable and unfailing.
Wherever all the Asuras and Andhaka, their foe in battle, moved,
from there the Pramathas fled in pieces along with the gods.
With his bow constantly drawn, like the sun encircled with a halo,
he poured forth multitudes of arrows as the sun pours down rays.

7.16.m:
Stricken by the pain of his arrows, like trees upon a riverbank,
all the leaders of the Gaṇas sank down, and so did the gods along with Indra.
Piercing Viṣṇu with a single arrow, Ananta with two, and Indra with three,
and tearing Yama, Soma, the lord of waters, and the Vasus, he roared terribly.
Having pierced the two Aśvins with two arrows, as well as Bhaga, Aṃśa, Aryaman, Candra, and Pūṣan,
then the doer of terrible deeds also mangled Nandīśvara and the Gaṇa leaders with his arrows.
Thus the violent Andhaka burned them, just as the blessed fire burns moths;
checked and torn by arrows then by Andhaka, those foremost warriors of the immortals
could neither move nor look upon Andhaka in battle, like men looking at the sun in the sky.
Then, abandoning their blazing glory, the gods, together with Nārāyaṇa and the guardians of the deities,
afflicted by arrows and exhausted from being pierced by the Dānava, fled before the wildfire of Andhaka.
Viṣṇu, the Grandfather [Brahmā], Ananta, and then Indra
were broken in battle by Andhaka with arrows resembling tongues of fire.
The Ādityas, Vasus, Sādhyas, and the two Aśvins, best of gods,
were broken in battle by Andhaka like birds by thunderbolts.
The Tuṣitas, the Viśvedevas, and the gods who partake of the ancestral offering
were broken by Andhaka with arrows, like trees by the wind.
The blessed Moon, Fire, the lord of wealth [Kubera], and the Rākṣasa [Nirṛti]
were broken in battle by Andhaka with arrows like venomous serpents.
Gandharvas, Guhyakas, serpents, Garuḍas, and great Nāgas
were broken in battle by Andhaka, pierced with arrows resembling fire.

7.16.m:
Viṭpati, Śaṅkukarṇa, Somanandī, Prabhāmaya,
Piṅgala, Nandiṣeṇa, Ghaṇṭākarṇa, Mahodara,
Vidyutkeśa, Sukeśa, and the god Vināyaka,
and other heroic Pramathas, headed by Vīrabhadra,
were broken in battle by Andhaka by the hundreds and thousands.
The entire threefold world, together with all moving and unmoving things, aroused to war
with Nārāyaṇa and the lord of gods, was routed in battle by Andhaka.
In that army of the gods, leaving aside the one god, the lord of the Gaṇas [Nandī],
whose crown bore a great crest-jewel, not a single one stood his ground.
Then in the Asura army arose a terrible, mighty lion-roar
raised by every creature, wondrous with the sound of musical instruments.
Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-fourth chapter in the Skandapurāṇa, on the victory of Andhaka.
Sanatkumāra said:
Meanwhile all the gods, headed by Indra,
accompanied by Brahmā, went to the trident-bearing refuge [Śiva].
Bowing down to Mahādeva, afflicted with fear, they said:
"We have all been utterly conquered! Why do you overlook Andhaka?"
The God of gods then replied to the gods headed by Brahmā:
"Because a boon was granted by me, therefore you were conquered.
And solely for sport was he ignored by me in the battle.
Now, for your sake, I shall destroy Andhaka."
Then the god, smiling, looked upon the trident standing by his side.
Knowing the true intention of the god, the trident blazed up in that very instant;
and advancing swiftly upon Andhaka, who vaunted his victory,
moving with power in battle, it suddenly pierced him through the chest.

Vyāsa said:
Having shown grace to Andhaka and dismissed the gods with their hosts, / tell me in truth what the Lord of the moving and unmoving then did.
Sanatkumāra said:
When the gods had gone to heaven, and Andhaka had been made a leader of attendants, / the Lord of gods, together with Andhaka, Nandi, and the Goddess […]
After a long time, the crescent-crowned sovereign of the pramathas entered his home / and gladdened it, as if it were the dwellings of Meru.
Hara, whose forehead-mark is the crescent moon, [beheld] his consort whose face resembles the moon;
she is seen in the midst of her companions like Rohiṇī among the stars.
Seeing the Lord of gods, whose banner bears the bull, having approached, / the Goddess too quickly rose from her seat along with her companions.
Placing her folded hands upon her head like a lotus bud, / she bowed to his feet with a delighted heart.
The Lord, too, having raised her up, along with her / sat down on a seat yellowish-red with the rays of jewels.
And out of a desire to please the Goddess, Śaṃkara told her / that Andhaka had been conquered in battle and, further, made an exalted attendant:

7.16.m:
“This Andhaka is your son, born from my very eyes; / he who had despised you has now been made to renounce his demonic nature.”
When the Lord of gods, Śaṃkara, had spoken thus, the dānava Andhaka, / bowing low with folded hands, made his petition to Pārvatī:
“O Goddess, I am Andhaka, who has received favor from the God, O auspicious one! / I have become your servant; look upon me with gentle eyes.
O Mother, forgive that transgression of mine against you, born of demonic nature. / I have received grace from the God, and I am your servant [ready for your] smile.
Patient, restrained, devoted, intent on taking refuge in you— / know me, O Mother, to be established in pure disposition.”
Having spoken thus to the mountain-born Goddess, Andhaka, resembling a mountain peak, / with propitiatory words praised her, bowing down with folded hands.

sported happily upon that mountain as he pleased.
Thus ends the one hundred fifty-seventh chapter, entitled 'Bestowal of a Boon to Andhaka', in the Skandapurāṇa.
Vyāsa said:
Having made Andhaka a leader of the gaṇas, what did Maheśvara do next
together with the goddess? Speak, and remove my curiosity!
Sanatkumāra said:
Having conquered Andhaka, O Vyāsa, and made him a leader of the gaṇas,
the remover of the gods' distress sported with the daughter of the king of mountains.

and in other such [hells], surrounded by their misdeeds,
punished on the order of Mṛtyu by rākṣasas of cruel deeds,
thus surrounded by terrifying evils and tormented by rākṣasas—
a good son rescues the ancestors, O goddess, not another who is bent on sin.

only one alone is here who rescues the ancestors from fear.

just as a vicious bull, or a eunuch [counts not as] king.

[Brahmā said:]
“… how you, [O trees,] stationary beings, shall establish in happiness
your ancestors who have reached hell and are afflicted by torments, learn that.
Whatever man, by rites and with sacred mantras,
performs in full your purificatory rites beginning with conception, and takes you as a son,
and those who, according to rule, make those previously born
and without an owner into adoptive sons—you shall deliver them as well.
You shall grant all desires and supreme happiness,
the destruction of karma for everyone, and imperishable worlds.”
Sanatkumāra said:
Then the daughter of the mountain asked again about that excellent rule.
To her asking, Mahādeva spoke this word:
“O goddess whose thighs are like an elephant-king’s trunk, walking with the gait of a lordly elephant,
hear the rule by which a tree is taken as a son.
‘Tomorrow, I shall adopt an earth-born [tree],’ O Pārvatī,
thinking thus, a woman should fast, possessing pure conduct and pure vows.
Then, when the sun of a hundred thousand rays has gone to the mountain of sunset,
and the spotless moon has risen, O moon-faced one,
in the supreme spirit of distress, O fortunate and supreme-souled lady,
she should invite at night pure brahmins who recite the Veda.
For they are mines of Vedic scriptures, like the oceans of jewels.
Brahmins, O woman whose face resembles the moon, are to be worshipped by the thousands.
Where brahmins who know mantras do not partake of the excellent offering,
there, O ruler of gods, the gods never eat the offering.
It does not spill, it does not suffer, and darkness does not overcome it;
this is the most distinguished of gifts: what is offered into the mouth of a brahmin.

taking food to be chewed and eaten, she should go where the tree stands.
Then the woman, following into the shadow of the tree,
having provided the young tree with a banner, a parasol, and ornaments,
and having fed the best of the twice-born with available food,
and having an auspicious-day declaration performed by the family priest or by herself,
having declared in truth her own intention to the satisfied brahmins
with supreme devotion, directing it toward the highest end:
‘I am childless, O venerable ones; I will take this tree
as an adoptive son. You ought to grant me your permission, O sinless ones.’
Then, with permission granted by them, O dear one,
before the earthly gods (brahmins) she should take that young tree as a son, O dear one.
A young tree taken as a son by this rule, O goddess,
showers honey and Soma upon ancestors dwelling in hell.
A tree adopted as a son by this rule, O fair-browed lady,
results in happiness, O auspicious one; [adopted] contrary [to rule], it brings pain.

When the gods cast away the fruit of a son, that sapling tree / will indeed become a son to me, childless as I am, bestowing contentment, O sinless one. (74)
To Bhavānī who spoke thus, the blessed Bhava, / the scorcher of foes, spoke words issuing from his true affection: (75)
O Goddess with eyes like blossoming lotuses, how indeed could there not be a son / for you, an ascetic woman, when I possess supreme sovereignty? (76)
You are capable of bearing sons through austerity, O blameless one; / and I too shall grant you most splendid sons. (77)

831 / 'So that tomorrow morning, O joyful Goddess, we may go together with Nandin to the side of the aśoka tree, arrange it thus, O Daughter of the Mountain King.'
'For there the entire world, together with the sky, waters, and Pātāla, O Mother of the universe, will be assembled for your welfare, O Daughter of the Mountain.'
'And by this Nandin, inviting the foremost of brahmins, the three strides of Nārāyaṇa, traversed by Trivikrama, were traversed.'
'Therefore, O fair-hipped lady, O choicest one, O giver of boons, I shall grant him a boon, O gracious one, if it pleases you, my beloved.' / Then the Goddess spoke to the Lord of heaven, Ḍiṇḍimuṇḍeśvara, Hara, the giver of boons, the beloved, adorned with the crescent moon:
'This Lord Nandin, O God, is our supreme benefactor. / He deserves thousands of crores of boons from you, without a doubt.'
'For you are the giver of boons to the worlds, and the Lord of the worlds as well. / If you are pleased, grant an excellent boon to the son of Śilāda.' / Then the God clad in animal hides, smelling Nandin on the crown of his head, / said to the Lord of the Pramathas: 'Choose a desired boon!'
